clue.text: Alarm when springtime comes to the underworld

parts.note: Dis is the Roman god of the underworld, and his realm
May is a month of spring

explanation.surface: A myth of spring arriving in the land of the dead, causing alarm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comes to' is only a link: the month follows the underworld's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Dismay is a sudden loss of courage, a synonym of alarm as a noun.

clue.text: Shadow over eye for two hours aboard ship

indicators.note: in a down clue over means the first word sits above the second

parts.note: to dog is to follow or shadow someone
to eye something is to watch it

explanation.surface: A detective trails a suspect and keeps an eye on him for a couple of hours at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The watch system at sea has two short two-hour shifts in the early evening, so the crew's duties rotate.
explanation.definitionFit: A dogwatch is either of two short spells of duty on a ship, from 4 to 6 or 6 to 8 pm.

clue.text: Cheese unnaturally high with this?

explanation.surface: A suspicion that a cheese has been artificially raised.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the cheese's name into two words: someone wearing a stilt is raised above natural height.
explanation.definitionFit: Stilton is a blue English cheese; split as 'stilt on', it describes one who walks unnaturally tall on poles.

clue.text: Such conviction covers life

explanation.surface: A believer's certainty is said to protect a whole lifetime.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain, insurance paying out on death is traditionally called life assurance, so the word for certainty also names the policy.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means firm certainty, and in Britain it also names the insurance policy that pays out on a death.

clue.text: A lady's undergarment is on the wrong way — there is chafing

parts.note: a bra is a woman's undergarment

indicators.note: the wrong way round means the little word is is read backwards

explanation.surface: A woman complains that her bra, put on back to front, is rubbing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the wrong way' turns IS into SI; 'there is' is a link before the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An abrasion is a scraping of the skin, the result of rubbing or chafing.

clue.text: Instructions to defender on field, lifting gear?

explanation.surface: A coach shouts orders to a defender before he is lifted off the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as two commands, the phrase tells a defender to obstruct and then tackle; as one term it is a pulley system for lifting.
explanation.definitionFit: A defender in football or rugby is told to stop and tackle opponents; the phrase also names pulleys and rope for hoisting.

clue.text: Boring thing to predict, we hear

indicators.note: we hear signals that the word for predicting is said out loud, and its sound gives the answer

parts.note: to augur is to foretell or predict

explanation.surface: A dull person tries to forecast the future, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' suggests dull, but it means drilling.
explanation.definitionFit: An auger is a tool for drilling holes, something that bores.

clue.text: Senseless, like Hamlet's life-story

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses the Prince of Denmark's biography as pointless.
explanation.walkthrough: The line 'a tale told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, signifying nothing' is spoken by Macbeth, not Hamlet; the setter has the wrong tragic hero.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiotic means stupid or senseless; Shakespeare called life 'a tale told by an idiot'.

clue.text: Calling with North American porcelain?

parts.note: Ming is fine Chinese porcelain from the Ming dynasty

explanation.surface: A dealer phones about a vase of American-owned Chinese porcelain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling something a name means labelling it, the act of giving a name.

clue.text: A perfect budget for an Oscar presentation

explanation.surface: An awards-night budget that is just right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oscar' is not the film award but Oscar Wilde, whose play was presented on stage; 'husband' as a verb means to manage resources thriftily.
explanation.definitionFit: To husband money is to budget it carefully, so a perfect budgeter fits; Oscar Wilde's comedy of 1895 bears the title.

clue.text: Sliding scale for trombonists?

parts.note: a trombone's slide lets a player run continuously up or down a scale; the economist's 'sliding scale' is read as a musical effect

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sliding scale' is the economics phrase for charges that vary; here it is a scale literally slid through by a trombonist.
explanation.definitionFit: A glissando is a rapid slide through successive notes, a trombone speciality.

clue.text: German folklorist, sinister, with male following

indicators.note: following says the letter for male comes after the word for sinister

parts.note: grim means forbidding or sinister

explanation.surface: A description of a dark-minded German collector of tales with a man behind him.
explanation.walkthrough: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm collected German folk tales.
explanation.definitionFit: The Brothers Grimm were the famous German collectors of fairy tales and folklore.

clue.text: Uniformed soldiers in retreat, fatigued

indicators.note: soldiers in retreat go backwards, so their letters are read in reverse

parts.note: TA is the Territorial Army, British reserve soldiers
fatigued means tired

explanation.surface: Weary soldiers in uniform falling back from the front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in retreat' turns TA into AT; 'fatigued' looks like it describes the soldiers but simply gives TIRED. 'Fatigues' is also army dress, which strengthens the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Attired means dressed, and someone in uniform is dressed in a set outfit.

clue.text: Nail-hardener used by tinker at Inishmaan

indicators.note: used by says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A travelling tinker on an Aran island uses something to harden nails.
explanation.walkthrough: Inishmaan is one of the Aran Islands off Ireland's west coast; the nails sound like a tinker's metal ones but are fingernails.
explanation.definitionFit: Keratin is the tough protein of which fingernails are made, giving them hardness.

clue.text: Priest to be Head of Chapter soon

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so take the opening letter of Chapter

parts.note: anon is an old word for soon

explanation.surface: A cleric expecting promotion to lead a cathedral chapter shortly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be' is a link; a cathedral chapter is its body of clergy, which gives the surface its sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A canon is a clergyman attached to a cathedral, a kind of priest.

clue.text: Intimate girl puts on a little weight

parts.note: Ann is a girl's name
an ounce is a small unit of weight

explanation.surface: A remark that a close girlfriend has gained a few grams.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Intimate' looks like an adjective describing the girl, but it is the verb meaning to make known; 'puts on' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To intimate is to state or make known, as to announce is to declare.

clue.text: Neat dude until shaken up

indicators.note: shaken up as a cocktail is shaken means these letters are mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: A smart fellow is tidy until something rattles him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neat' looks like tidy, but it is the barman's sense of a drink with nothing added; 'shaken up' rearranges DUDE and UNTIL.
explanation.definitionFit: A neat spirit is served without water or mixer, so it is not watered down.

clue.text: Sticks on pitch, a centre of attraction

indicators.note: in a down clue on means the first word sits above the second

parts.note: poles are long sticks
pitch is a black sticky substance, tar

explanation.surface: Stumps placed on a cricket pitch draw all eyes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pitch' suggests a sports field, but it is the black sticky substance.
explanation.definitionFit: The North Star is a fixed guiding point, so the word is used for anything that draws people.

clue.text: How team's beaten'? Rather!

indicators.note: beaten as eggs are beaten means these letters are whisked into a new order

parts.note: the possessive is taken as its letters, giving the S

explanation.surface: A fan asks how badly the side lost and gets an emphatic reply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beaten' rearranges HOW and TEAMS into the answer; the exclamation 'Rather!' is old British slang for an emphatic yes, but the definition uses its other sense, to some degree.
explanation.definitionFit: Rather, meaning to a certain degree or fairly, is a synonym of the adverb used here.

clue.text: Month at work for an ink manufacturer

parts.note: Oct is short for October
an opus is a work of art or music

explanation.surface: A busy October at a factory making ink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at' is a link; the 'ink manufacturer' is a sea creature that squirts ink.
explanation.definitionFit: The octopus produces a cloud of dark fluid to escape predators.

clue.text: Reversing vehicle in event, his penalties were terrible

indicators.note: in places the turned car inside the word for event

parts.note: a do is a party or social event

indicators.note: reversing a vehicle backs it up, so the word for the car is read backwards

parts.note: a car is a vehicle

explanation.surface: A driver backing up at a gathering, with harsh punishment following.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reversing' turns the car into RAC. Draco was an Athenian lawmaker whose code was so harsh that 'draconian' now means severe.
explanation.definitionFit: Draco's ancient Athenian laws prescribed death for minor offences, giving the adjective draconian.

clue.text: Bait men throw out, creating relaxing atmosphere

indicators.note: the anglers throw the bait out, and the throw scatters these letters into a new order

explanation.surface: Anglers cast their bait and settle into a calm mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'throw out' rearranges BAIT and MEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambient music or lighting is designed to set a calm, soothing mood in the surroundings.

clue.text: A born leader profits by exploits

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, so take the opening letter of born

parts.note: to profit by something is to use it

explanation.surface: A natural leader gains from his own achievements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exploits' looks like a noun for deeds, but it is the verb meaning takes unfair advantage of.
explanation.definitionFit: To exploit someone is to take unfair advantage of them, which is to misuse or ill-treat.

clue.text: Works on Graves in chateau?

parts.note: Graves is a Bordeaux wine region; at the chateau the wine is put into glass, which reads like a scholar writing studies of the poet Robert Graves

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests books or essays about the writer Robert Graves; 'Works' means the things made, and Graves is wine, put into containers at the chateau.
explanation.definitionFit: Wine from the Graves region is filled into glass containers at the producing estate.

clue.text: The French hail-and-farewell

parts.note: le is French for the
ave is the Latin greeting, hail

explanation.surface: A Frenchman's greeting and goodbye in one breath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking one's leave means saying goodbye, so the noun serves as a farewell.

clue.text: Distinction of some lines in Alice perhaps

indicators.note: in places the railway letters inside the rearranged name
perhaps signals that the name may appear in some other arrangement of its letters

parts.note: BR, British Rail, owned a network of railway lines

explanation.surface: Praise for the quality of certain lines in Lewis Carroll's Alice books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges the name to CALIE, and 'in' puts the railway letters inside it before the final E; the lines are rail tracks, not lines of verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Calibre means quality or excellence of character, a sense shared with distinction.

clue.text: Mince-pies a brown colour

indicators.note: to mince is to chop up finely, so the following letters are chopped and reordered

explanation.surface: A remark that mince pies come out of the oven brown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mince-pies' looks like the Christmas pastry, but 'Mince' is the anagram signal working on PIES and A.
explanation.definitionFit: Sepia is a reddish-brown pigment, originally from cuttlefish ink, and its tint.

clue.text: Stint in kitchen-garden

explanation.surface: A spell of work done in the vegetable patch.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a council rents out small plots for growing vegetables; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A stint is an allotted portion or share; a rented vegetable plot in Britain is also called by this name.

clue.text: Postpones putting drains around America

indicators.note: around says the word for drains is wrapped round the letters for America

parts.note: to drain funds is to spend them
US is short for the United States, America

explanation.surface: A plumber delays fitting drainpipes around the American site.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drains' looks like pipes, but it is the verb, as when a purchase drains (spends) money.
explanation.definitionFit: To suspend a meeting or sentence is to defer or put it off for a time.

clue.text: Tried oxygen to restore journalist in charge?

indicators.note: restore means to put back into a fresh order, so these letters are rebuilt

parts.note: O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A patient was given oxygen to revive a senior newsman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to restore' rearranges TRIED and O.
explanation.definitionFit: The person in charge of a newspaper and its journalists is its chief, the paper's senior editorial figure.
